791.event_title: The eunuch Wang Zhen leads the Zhengtong Emperor into disaster at Tumu
791.place: Tumu, near present-day Huailai, Hebei, China
791.event: The young Zhengtong Emperor of the Ming dynasty placed his complete trust in the eunuch Wang Zhen, his first teacher, who came to dominate the government. In 1449, when the Oirat Mongol leader Esen invaded, Wang Zhen persuaded the emperor to lead an army against him in person, overriding the objections of senior ministers and officers. At the Tumu post station the ill-prepared Ming army was surrounded and largely destroyed, and the emperor was captured and held by the Mongols for about a year.
791.explanation: The disaster weakened the Ming dynasty and showed how costly a ruler's unexamined trust in a favourite could be.
791.tie_back: The kural warns that nothing is more harmful than friendship formed without careful examination, because a loyal person cannot afterwards break free of it, and the emperor's unquestioning bond with Wang Zhen led him straight into captivity.
791._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the harm of an unexamined attachment; the bond was between a ruler and a servant-tutor rather than between equals.

792.event_title: Pompey seeks refuge with the court of Ptolemy XIII
792.event: After his defeat by Julius Caesar at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BC, Pompey the Great fled to Egypt, seeking refuge with the young king Ptolemy XIII, whose family had long-standing ties to him. The king's courtiers, wishing to win the favour of the victorious Caesar, decided to be rid of their guest, and Pompey was killed as he came ashore by men sent to meet him.
792.explanation: Pompey relied on an old connection without weighing the men who now held power at the Egyptian court, and that misplaced trust cost him his life.
792.tie_back: The kural warns that a friendship not examined again and again can bring, in the end, sorrow enough to kill, and Pompey's untested reliance on his Egyptian ties did exactly that.
792._accuracy_note: Partial fit: Pompey trusted a political connection rather than a personal friend, though the outcome matches the kural's warning closely.

793.event_title: Britain introduces positive vetting after the Burgess and Maclean defections
793.event: In 1951 the British diplomats Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean, who had been recruited by Soviet intelligence before the Second World War, defected to the Soviet Union. In response, the British government in 1952 introduced positive vetting, a procedure intended to establish the integrity of civil servants doing exceptionally secret work. Earlier screening had focused on Communist or Fascist sympathies and associations, but positive vetting widened the inquiry to a person's character, and in 1956 the government declared publicly that character defects could affect a civil servant's posting or promotion.
793.explanation: The reform reflected a hard lesson: trusted men had been given access to vital secrets without anyone examining closely their character and associations.
793.tie_back: The kural advises learning a person's character, background, faults and associates before admitting him to close friendship, and positive vetting applied that same examination before admitting a person to the state's secrets.
793._accuracy_note: Close on examining character and associates before trusting someone, but the setting is state security rather than personal friendship.

794.event_title: Catherine the Great buys Diderot's library and leaves it with him
794.place: Paris, France, and St Petersburg, Russia
794.event: In 1765 Catherine the Great learned that the French philosopher Denis Diderot, editor of the Encyclopedie, was about to sell his library to provide a dowry for his daughter. She bought the collection for 15,000 livres on condition that the books remain with Diderot for the rest of his life, and paid him a yearly sum as librarian of his own books. Diderot afterwards recruited scholars and artists on her behalf and, in 1773, travelled to St Petersburg, where he met the empress for long conversations.
794.explanation: Catherine was willing to pay generously to win the friendship and goodwill of one of the most respected thinkers in Europe.
794.tie_back: The kural advises securing, even at a price, the friendship of a worthy person who shrinks from disgrace, and Catherine quite literally paid to gain Diderot's friendship.
794._accuracy_note: Close on paying to win a worthy friend, but Diderot was not of noble birth and Catherine's motives were partly about prestige, so the fit is partial.

795.event_title: Clementine Churchill's frank letter to Winston
795.event: On 27 June 1940, in the weeks after the fall of France, Clementine Churchill wrote to her husband, now Prime Minister, to warn him that he was in danger of becoming unpopular with his colleagues and staff because of his rough, sarcastic and overbearing manner. She told him plainly that she herself had noticed his manner growing worse, and urged him to combine his great power with kindness and calm. The letter is preserved in the Churchill Archives Centre at Churchill College, Cambridge.
795.explanation: The letter is remembered as a model of loving but unsparing counsel, offered to the most powerful man in Britain at a moment of extreme strain.
795.tie_back: Valluvar urges us to seek those who can speak hard words that sting and who understand the ways of the world, and Clementine's letter was exactly such counsel.
795._accuracy_note: Strong on frank, painful counsel from someone wise in the world; the counsellor was a wife rather than a friend, though she was passing on a friend's warning.

796.event_title: Mark Twain publishes the memoirs of the ruined Ulysses S. Grant
796.event: In May 1884 the collapse of the Wall Street firm of Grant & Ward, run by his partner Ferdinand Ward, wiped out former President Ulysses S. Grant's savings, and later that year he learned that he had incurable throat cancer. His friend Mark Twain, who had long urged him to write his memoirs, arranged to publish them through his own publishing firm, and Grant raced to finish the manuscript, completing it only days before his death in July 1885. The memoirs sold about 300,000 sets and earned his widow, Julia, more than 400,000 dollars.
796.explanation: When Grant lost his fortune and faced death, Twain's friendship provided the means by which he saved his family from poverty.
796.tie_back: The kural says that even ruin has one benefit, since it is a measuring rod that shows how far one's friends truly reach, and Grant's ruin showed the full length of Twain's friendship.
796._accuracy_note: Strong fit on misfortune revealing a true friend, though the sources do not record others who abandoned Grant for contrast.

797.event_title: Gandhi breaks with his boyhood companion Sheikh Mehtab
797.event: As a schoolboy in Rajkot, Mohandas Gandhi formed a close friendship with Sheikh Mehtab, entering it, as he later wrote, in the spirit of a reformer, and he described it in his autobiography in two chapters titled A Tragedy. Mehtab later lived in Gandhi's household in Durban, where Gandhi discovered serious misconduct by him and learned that he had turned Gandhi against an honest clerk with false suspicions. Gandhi told him he would have nothing more to do with him and made him leave the house, later writing that in trying to reform the man he had nearly ruined himself and that the break let him begin a more detached and disciplined life.
797.explanation: Gandhi came to see the end of this friendship not as a loss but as a rescue that freed him for his later work.
797.tie_back: The kural says the real gain for a person is to give up completely the friendship of fools, and Gandhi himself described his break with Mehtab as a deliverance.
797._accuracy_note: Close fit, told largely in Gandhi's own words; one source is the autobiography itself, the other a scholar's identification of the companion as Mehtab.

798.event_title: Charles I abandons the Earl of Strafford
798.event: Thomas Wentworth, Earl of Strafford, had become King Charles I's chief adviser and in 1641 was impeached by the Long Parliament. When his trial failed to prove treason, his opponents turned to a bill of attainder, and after anguished hesitation Charles, fearing for his own security, gave his assent to it. Strafford was executed on Tower Hill on 12 May 1641.
798.explanation: Strafford had served the king with total devotion, yet in the crisis Charles let him die to protect himself, a decision the king later came to regard as a grave sin.
798.tie_back: The kural warns against taking up the friendship of those who will cut you off when trouble comes, and Strafford gave everything to a master who deserted him at the decisive moment.
798._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of a friend withdrawing support in the hour of need, though the bond was between king and servant.

799.event_title: Napoleon names Marmont's betrayal in his last will
799.event: Auguste Marmont had been one of Napoleon's closest companions since meeting him at the siege of Toulon in 1793, serving as his aide-de-camp and later becoming a marshal. In April 1814, with Napoleon's position collapsing, Marmont went over to the Allies with his army corps, a defection that helped force Napoleon's abdication and made the word ragusade, from Marmont's title of duke of Ragusa, a byword for treachery. In exile on St Helena, as his strength was failing, Napoleon wrote out his will on 15 April 1821, and in it he named Marmont first among those whose treason he blamed for the invasions of France, while declaring that he forgave them.
799.explanation: Even in his final weeks, Napoleon's mind returned to the old friend who had abandoned him at his fall.
799.tie_back: The kural says the memory of friends who abandoned you when you were falling will burn the heart even at the hour of death, and Napoleon named Marmont's desertion in his last will.
799._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a deserting friend still on the dying man's mind in his final testament.

800.event_title: Eisenhower accepts the resignation of Sherman Adams
800.event: In 1958 a congressional subcommittee revealed that Sherman Adams, President Dwight D. Eisenhower's chief of staff, had accepted gifts, including a vicuna coat and an oriental rug, as well as hotel bills from his old friend Bernard Goldfine, a New England textile manufacturer in trouble with federal regulators, and that Adams had contacted those agencies about Goldfine's cases. Eisenhower at first defended Adams publicly, but as pressure from his own party mounted before the 1958 elections, Adams resigned, and Eisenhower accepted the resignation with deep regret on 22 September 1958.
800.explanation: Adams's career was lost to an unwise friendship, and Eisenhower had to give up his most valued aide to protect his administration.
800.tie_back: The kural urges us to cling to the blameless and to let go of unsuitable associations even at a cost, and Eisenhower paid the price of losing an aide he greatly valued because of Adams's ties to Goldfine.
800._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the parting was forced by political pressure rather than chosen on principle, though it shows the cost of an unsuitable friendship.
